body:
What Gaganyaan is intended to demonstrate

Gaganyaan is the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) programme to demonstrate India's capability to send people into low Earth orbit (LEO) using an Indian launch vehicle and bring them back safely. It is a human spaceflight programme, not a mission to land on the Moon or to place astronauts permanently in space.

The stated crewed-mission plan is to send 3 astronauts to an orbit about 400 km above Earth for about 3 days and return the crew module to Indian sea waters.

Why the spacecraft can remain in orbit

A satellite is a body that moves around another body under gravity. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite; a spacecraft placed around Earth is an artificial satellite. A launch vehicle provides the speed and height needed to enter orbit. After insertion, Earth's gravity continuously changes the spacecraft's direction so that it moves around the planet rather than simply travelling in a straight line.

Orbiting astronauts experience microgravity, often called apparent weightlessness, because they and the spacecraft are falling together around Earth. Gravity has not disappeared at an altitude of 400 km. This distinction explains why a human spaceflight mission still requires careful control of motion, atmosphere and crew safety.

What makes a human mission different

An uncrewed satellite mainly has to keep its instruments working. A crewed spacecraft must also maintain a breathable cabin environment, protect people during launch and re-entry, provide escape arrangements for emergencies, and permit the crew to be found and recovered after landing. These requirements explain why Gaganyaan uses several tests before carrying astronauts.

Prelims focus

  • Agency: Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).
  • Mission type: human spaceflight to low Earth orbit, not a lunar landing.
  • Stated crewed plan: 3 astronauts, about 400 km altitude, about 3 days.
  • Return method: recovery from designated Indian sea waters.
  • Trap: An astronaut in orbit is not beyond Earth's gravity.

[Sources: ISRO, Gaganyaan programme overview, 23 November 2022, sections 'Gaganyaan' and 'Human rated LVM3'; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 1 'The Earth in the Solar System', printed pp. 4–5, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 9, chapter 10 'Gravitation', printed pp. 131–134, 2018–19 reprint; consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
How the mission components fit together

The Human-Rated LVM3 (HLVM3) is the launch vehicle planned to carry Gaganyaan's spacecraft into orbit. It is an adapted version of ISRO's LVM3 rocket, with measures intended to meet the higher safety and reliability demands of carrying humans. The LVM3 family uses solid, liquid and cryogenic propulsion stages. The rocket supplies the initial journey to space; it is not the astronauts' living compartment.

The spacecraft that travels in orbit is the Orbital Module (OM). It consists of 2 different parts: the Crew Module (CM) and the Service Module (SM). They operate together during the orbital phase but do different jobs.

The Crew Module is the habitable and returning part

The Crew Module is a pressurised cabin where astronauts can live and work in an Earth-like internal environment. It contains crew controls and essential life-support equipment. Its Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) is designed to maintain conditions such as a suitable cabin atmosphere and temperature. The Crew Module also has protection against the intense heating associated with atmospheric re-entry and a system to slow its final descent.

The fact that the full crewed Crew Module is pressurised does not mean every test article is pressurised. ISRO's TV-D1 test used an unpressurised test crew module to examine escape and recovery functions; no astronaut was aboard.

The Service Module supports the mission in orbit

The Service Module is unpressurised. It provides systems needed to support the Crew Module during orbital operations, including power, propulsion, temperature control and associated electronics. Its job differs from the Crew Module's job: the Service Module supports the flight, while the Crew Module houses and ultimately returns the people.

The Crew Escape System is for an emergency

The Crew Escape System (CES) is designed to pull the Crew Module clear of the launch vehicle if a dangerous situation occurs at the launch pad or during ascent. It should not be confused with the Service Module, which supports normal orbital operations, or with the parachutes, which slow the returning capsule near the end of descent.

CM: crew lives and returns. SM: supports the crew module in orbit. CES: separates the crew module from danger during a launch emergency. HLVM3: carries the spacecraft towards orbit.

Prelims focus

  • Gaganyaan launch vehicle: Human-Rated LVM3 (HLVM3).
  • Orbital Module = Crew Module + Service Module.
  • Crew Module: pressurised, habitable, designed for re-entry and return.
  • Service Module: unpressurised, provides orbital support.
  • Crew Escape System: safety during a launch-pad or ascent emergency.
  • Trap: The crew does not live inside the Service Module.

[Sources: ISRO, Gaganyaan programme overview, 23 November 2022, sections 'Human rated LVM3' and 'Orbital Module'; ISRO, 'First Crew Module for Gaganyaan test flight takes shape', 6 October 2023; ISRO, 'Crew Module–Service Module Separation Tests', 16 October 2026; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: The Spacecraft: HLVM3, Crew Module, Service Module and Escape System

body:
Normal flight: 3 broad phases

ISRO divides the planned human mission into ascent, orbital flight and descent. The phases have different purposes. The launch vehicle first carries the spacecraft towards orbit. The orbital module then operates in space. Finally, the crew module makes a controlled return to Earth.

  1. Ascent: HLVM3 lifts off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota and carries the Orbital Module towards low Earth orbit. The Crew Escape System provides a possible emergency escape route during the dangerous early part of the flight.
  2. Orbital flight: The spacecraft reaches the required orbit around Earth. The mission plan calls for a roughly 400 km orbit and approximately 3 days in space. Astronauts remain in the pressurised Crew Module, supported by the Service Module.
  3. Preparing to return: A controlled change in the spacecraft's motion, called a de-boost manoeuvre, begins the return from orbit. Before atmospheric re-entry, the Crew Module separates from the Service Module.
  4. Re-entry: The Crew Module passes into denser atmospheric layers. Its thermal protection system is designed to shield it from severe re-entry heating.
  5. Descent and recovery: A parachute-based system reduces the Crew Module's speed for splashdown at a designated location in Indian sea waters. Recovery teams then locate and retrieve the capsule and its occupants.

Why safe return is part of mission success

Putting a spacecraft into orbit is only one part of human spaceflight capability. Gaganyaan must also demonstrate safe separation of the returning module, survival during re-entry and recovery after landing. A spacecraft that reaches orbit but cannot return the crew safely would not fulfil the programme's central objective.

Tests involving the Indian Navy have examined how a crew module can be retrieved after sea landing. Some uncrewed test capsules have been recovered in the Bay of Bengal near Sriharikota. That test location should not be treated as proof that every future crewed flight must land at exactly the same point.

Normal return and emergency abort are different: In a planned return, the spacecraft leaves orbit and the Crew Module descends. In an early-flight emergency, the Crew Escape System may separate the Crew Module from its rocket before it ever reaches orbit.

Prelims focus

  • The 3 broad phases are ascent, orbital flight and descent.
  • The Crew Module separates from the Service Module before re-entry.
  • The thermal protection system protects the returning module from re-entry heating.
  • Parachutes slow the Crew Module before splashdown.
  • Trap: A flight abort does not imply that the spacecraft has entered orbit.

[Sources: ISRO/Department of Space, Annual Report 2025–2026, section 2.6 'Gaganyaan', printed pp. 106–107; ISRO, Gaganyaan programme overview, sections 'Human rated LVM3' and 'Orbital Module'; ISRO, 'Integrated Air Drop Test for Gaganyaan Missions', 24 August 2025; ISRO, 'Second Integrated Air Drop Test', 10 April 2026; consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
Why tests come before astronauts

Human-rated space systems are assessed through separate tests before a crewed flight. Each test answers a different safety question: Can the capsule escape danger at launch? Can it separate during flight? Will parachutes slow it safely? Can the module be recovered after landing? A successful test demonstrates the tested capability under those conditions; it is not the same as completing a full crewed orbital mission.

Major completed tests

  • 5 July 2018 — Pad Abort Test (PAT): ISRO demonstrated the Crew Escape System's ability to take a simulated Crew Module away from a dangerous situation at the launch pad and return it under parachutes. The vehicle was not sent into orbit.
  • 21 October 2023 — Test Vehicle-D1 (TV-D1): A special test vehicle demonstrated an in-flight abort. It evaluated the Crew Escape System, separation of the test module and safe recovery. This was a suborbital safety test, not a human mission or an orbital Gaganyaan flight.
  • 24 August 2025 — Integrated Air Drop Test-01 (IADT-01): A helicopter released a simulated Crew Module so the parachute-based descent and sea recovery arrangements could be tested together.
  • 10 April 2026 — Integrated Air Drop Test-02 (IADT-02): Another simulated Crew Module was released from a helicopter near Sriharikota. The system used 10 parachutes of 4 types during descent; the module splashed down and was recovered with Indian Navy support.
  • 16 October 2026 — Crew Module–Service Module separation tests: ISRO reported successful ground tests of the mechanism that separates the 2 spacecraft modules before re-entry. A ground separation test is not itself a spaceflight.

What remained to be demonstrated

The next planned Test Vehicle mission, TV-D2, was still in preparation in the official programme updates available by 4 November 2026. The broader mission also requires complete uncrewed orbital flights before astronauts are carried. This is why a report of a successful pad-abort or parachute test must not be confused with the launch of Gaganyaan's first human crew.

Prelims focus

  • PAT: 5 July 2018; emergency escape at launch pad.
  • TV-D1: 21 October 2023; in-flight crew escape, suborbital.
  • IADT-01: 24 August 2025; parachute descent and recovery.
  • IADT-02: 10 April 2026; parachute descent and recovery, with 10 parachutes of 4 types.
  • CM–SM separation ground tests: reported successful on 16 October 2026.
  • Trap: TV-D1 was not the first uncrewed orbital mission G1.

[Sources: ISRO, 'Successful Flight Testing of Crew Escape System — Technology Demonstrator', 5 July 2018; ISRO, Gaganyaan TV-D1 Mission, mission definition and objectives, with actual flight date confirmed in ISRO October 2023 Department of Space monthly summary; ISRO, 'Integrated Air Drop Test', 24 August 2025; ISRO, 'Second Integrated Air Drop Test', 10 April 2026; ISRO, 'Crew Module–Service Module Separation Tests', 16 October 2026; PIB/Department of Space, 'Key Milestones in Gaganyaan', 6 August 2026; consulted 4 November 2026.]
